title: Can a single try have multiple catch blocks, and why must more specific exceptions be caught before more general ones (unreachable-catch compile error)?
shortTitle: Multiple catch blocks + ordering — specific before general, multi-catch (|)

s1_definition.profdef: YES — a single try can have MULTIPLE catch blocks, each handling a different exception type. They are checked TOP-TO-BOTTOM: the FIRST matching catch executes. RULE: specific exceptions MUST come BEFORE general ones. If `catch (Exception e)` is first, it catches EVERYTHING — subsequent catches like `catch (IOException e)` are UNREACHABLE → COMPILE ERROR. Java 7 added MULTI-CATCH: `catch (IOException | SQLException e)` — one block handles multiple unrelated exceptions. The caught variable is implicitly FINAL in multi-catch (can't reassign `e`).
s1_definition.analogy: Three complaint counters: Counter 1 handles "insufficient funds" (specific). Counter 2 handles "any transaction error" (general). Counter 3 handles "everything else." If you put "everything else" FIRST — nobody ever reaches Counter 1 or 2! The general counter catches ALL complaints. Java prevents this: specific FIRST, general LAST. Multi-catch (|): "Counter 1 handles BOTH insufficient funds AND invalid account" — one counter, two complaint types.
s1_definition.oneliner: Multiple catches: specific FIRST, general LAST. catch(Exception) before catch(IOException) → COMPILE ERROR (unreachable). Multi-catch: catch (IOException | SQLException e) — one block, multiple types, variable is final.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** YES — a single try can have MULTIPLE catch blocks, each handling a different exception type. They are checked TOP-TO-BOTTOM: the FIRST matching catch executes. RULE: specific exceptions MUST come BEFORE general ones. If `catch (Exception e)` is first, it catches EVERYTHING — subsequent catches like `catch (IOException e)` are UNREACHABLE → COMPILE ERROR. Java 7 added MULTI-CATCH: `catch (IOException | SQLException e)` — one block handles multiple unrelated exceptions. The caught variable is implicitly FINAL in multi-catch (can't reassign `e`).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Three complaint counters: Counter 1 handles "insufficient funds" (specific). Counter 2 handles "any transaction error" (general). Counter 3 handles "everything else." If you put "everything else" FIRST — nobody ever reaches Counter 1 or 2! The general counter catches ALL complaints. Java prevents this: specific FIRST, general LAST. Multi-catch (|): "Counter 1 handles BOTH insufficient funds AND invalid account" — one counter, two complaint types.

**One line to remember:** Multiple catches: specific FIRST, general LAST. catch(Exception) before catch(IOException) → COMPILE ERROR (unreachable). Multi-catch: catch (IOException | SQLException e) — one block, multiple types, variable is final.

sections.s3_banking: Problem — the trade file processor reads a daily trades CSV and persists it to the database, and a single operation can fail in several different ways: the file may be missing (FileNotFoundException), a general read may fail (IOException), the database write may fail (SQLException), or a parsing bug may throw a RuntimeException. A developer put `catch (Exception e)` first and then tried to add a more specific `catch (IOException e)` below it, and the code would not compile — the general catch made the specific one unreachable. Fix: order the catch blocks from MOST specific to LEAST specific so each exception reaches the handler that knows how to deal with it, which also matches the IS-A hierarchy the compiler enforces. This mini-project builds the processor with correctly ordered catches and a multi-catch variant, plus a JUnit test for each failure type.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four requests to the file processor — "notfound.csv", "ioerror.csv", "sqlerror.csv", and "nullbug.csv" — plus one valid file.

**Step 1.** The "notfound.csv" request enters `processWithCorrectOrder`. The processor throws FileNotFoundException. The catch blocks are checked top to bottom, and because the MOST specific handler (`catch (FileNotFoundException e)`) is first, it matches and returns the CATCH-1 result.

**Step 2.** The "ioerror.csv" request throws a plain IOException. The first catch (FileNotFoundException) does not match, so control falls to the second catch (`catch (IOException e)`), which is the parent type, and returns CATCH-2. This ordering works only because the child was listed before the parent.

**Step 3.** The "sqlerror.csv" request throws SQLException, an unrelated type, matched by the third catch; the "nullbug.csv" request throws a RuntimeException, matched by the fourth. Each exception reaches exactly the handler meant for it.

**Step 4.** Had `catch (Exception e)` been placed first, the compiler would reject the later `catch (IOException e)` as unreachable code. The multi-catch variant collapses the IOException and SQLException handlers into one block for the cases that share a body. The test verifies each path reaches its intended catch.

```
WARNING 2026-10-22T21:06:45 FileProcessor notfound.csv -> CATCH-1 FileNotFound
WARNING 2026-10-22T21:06:45 FileProcessor ioerror.csv  -> CATCH-2 IOException
WARNING 2026-10-22T21:06:45 FileProcessor sqlerror.csv -> CATCH-3 SQLException
WARNING 2026-10-22T21:06:45 FileProcessor nullbug.csv  -> CATCH-4 Runtime
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ CATCH ORDER: SPECIFIC → GENERAL ═══

  try { code }
  catch (FileNotFoundException e) { }   ← FIRST: most specific
  catch (IOException e) { }             ← SECOND: parent of FileNotFound
  catch (SQLException e) { }            ← THIRD: unrelated
  catch (Exception e) { }               ← LAST: catch-all

  FileNotFoundException thrown → matches FIRST catch ✅
  IOException thrown → skips first (not FileNotFound), matches SECOND ✅
  Exception general → matches LAST ✅

  ❌ WRONG: catch(Exception) before catch(IOException) → COMPILE ERROR!

  ═══ MULTI-CATCH (Java 7) ═══

  catch (IOException | SQLException e) { }
  ONE block, TWO exception types, variable is FINAL.
  Types must be UNRELATED (not parent-child).
```

       │  one try → multiple catch (checked TOP → BOTTOM)
       ├─ catch (FileNotFoundException)  ← MOST specific first
       ├─ catch (IOException)            ← parent after child
       ├─ catch (SQLException)
       └─ catch (Exception)              ← LEAST specific last

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  Exception
   └─ IOException
       └─ FileNotFoundException      ← IS-A IOException (child)
  Ordering (checked top-to-bottom):
    try { loadDoc(); persist(); }
    catch (FileNotFoundException e){ ... }   // child FIRST (legal)
    catch (IOException e)         { ... }     // parent AFTER child
    catch (SQLException e)        { ... }
    catch (Exception e)           { ... }     // catch-all LAST
  ❌ catch(Exception) first → every later catch UNREACHABLE (compile err)
  Multi-catch: catch (IOException | SQLException e) → e implicitly final,
               types must NOT be parent-child.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A single try can have multiple catch blocks checked top-to-bottom. Specific exceptions MUST come before general ones — if `catch (Exception e)` is first, all subsequent catches are unreachable (compile error). The rule follows the IS-A hierarchy: FileNotFoundException IS-A IOException, so catching IOException first would catch both — making the FileNotFoundException catch unreachable. Java 7 multi-catch `catch (IOException | SQLException e)` handles multiple UNRELATED exception types in one block. The caught variable is implicitly final — can't reassign. Multi-catch types must NOT have a parent-child relationship.
